extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Romantic-era literary criticism; literary critics and writers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted guidance and evaluative statements for writing criticism, poetry appraisal, and descriptive travel-letters; includes prescriptions on how to write and judge reviews, characterize speakers, and render scenes. Covers both ethical/practical rules for critics and stylistic techniques for descriptive/travel prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews should be personal, sharp, and pointed
rubrics_metrics.description: A Review, in order to be a saleable article, must be personal, sharp, and pointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that reviewers often become personal because that style sells; contextualizes the personal attack on Wordsworth as an example of reviewers making the author and his circle the object of revenge. Implies that visibility/market considerations drive this form of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for provocation when judging an author's indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let not Mr. Wordsworth be charged with having expressed himself too indignantly, till the wantonness and the systematic and malignant perseverance of the aggressions have been taken into fair consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an author's tone (indignation, anger), consider the severity and persistence of the attacks that prompted it; judgement of tone must factor in provocation and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism must present opinions supported by reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: I have advanced no opinion either for praise or censure, other than as texts introductory to the reasons which compel me to form it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic should not merely assert praise or blame; opinions should be stated as starting points and followed by the reasons and analysis that justify them—criticism should be argumentative and explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execute analytic criticism with adequate ability for constructive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a criticism was not only wanted; but that, if executed with adequate ability, it must conduce in no mean degree to Mr. Wordsworth's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic/constructive criticism, if skilfully done, benefits the author's reputation—criticism should be substantive and capable rather than merely hostile or superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh defects against beauties; defects don't imply lack of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: How small the proportion of the defects are to the beauties... and that no one of them originates in deficiency of poetic genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider the relative proportion of faults to merits and avoid inferring a lack of poetic genius from the presence of defects; contextual balancing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic/affected praise that mischaracterizes simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: I am disgusted with the gilded side of the same meaning, as displayed by some affected admirers with whom he is, forsooth, 'a sweet, simple poet!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware two-sided error: enemies who call a poet vulgar, and admirers who flatten complexity into sentimental 'simplicity'. Praise should be nuanced and not romanticize or sanitize the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use criticism to maliciously ruin an author
rubrics_metrics.description: They exert indeed power ... to write down, and (where the author's circumstances permit) to impoverish the man ... to make it impossible for the man even to publish any future work without exposing himself to all the wretchedness of debt and embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical critics should avoid using their influence to systematically ruin an author's livelihood; fairness and honesty are implicit obligations of critical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose settings that elicit social interaction and revealing detail
rubrics_metrics.description: I am inclined to believe that a packet is far superior to a stage-coach, as a means of making men open out to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For travel-letters or scenes where character revelation through talk is desired, prefer settings (e.g., packet ship) that encourage extended interaction and disclosure rather than transient, dozing environments (e.g., stage-coach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take notes to capture conversation and distinctive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: I determined, for once in my life to take notes of a conversation. Here it follows, somewhat abridged indeed, but in all other respects as accurately as my memory permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To render dialogue faithfully and preserve idiosyncrasies of speech, record conversations (notes) promptly rather than relying solely on memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render accents and character through phonetic/dialectal speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dane's speech is given in strongly accented, phonetic forms ('Vat imagination! vat language! vat vast science! ... Is I not veiy eloquent? Is I not speak English very fine?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using phonetic spelling, altered syntax, and repeated characteristic words can convey nationality, vanity, or comic effect; the Dane's long quoted speech is an explicit example of this technique (but author also signals the comedic and caricatured risks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid sensory detail and metaphor to convey landscape and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions such as the moonlight road on the water, a 'huge volume of deep black cloud,' spires that 'point as with silent fingers to the sky', and the 'little stars of flame' in foam are used to evoke setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensory images, metaphor, and specific local details (light, cloud, spire, foam) to create atmosphere; contrasts of light/dark and movement add emotional resonance to travel description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdote and personal incident to illustrate manners and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prussian's profane but witty anecdotes 'were valuable as illustrating the manners of the countries in which they had taken place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including short personal stories or recounted incidents can effectively illustrate national manners, character traits, or social mores—useful material for travel writing and character portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasts (silence vs noise; land vs sea) to heighten interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'striking contrast between the silence of this majestic stream... and the ceaseless noise, and uproar, and loud agitations of the desolate solitude of the ocean' is highlighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtaposing opposing elements (quiet river banks vs loud ocean solitude; spired town vs desolate sea) sharpens perception and helps the reader appreciate particular qualities of each scene.
